The self-service kiosk went in beside the window at the county housing assistance office, angled so that from her stool behind the glass she could read every line of it and hear whatever people muttered at it while they typed.

Her name was on the placard at the window. She had outlasted three program directors, one asbestos remediation, and the year the phones didn't work. Her job, boiled down, was to find out in ninety seconds what a person needed and whether this building was capable of giving it to them. Utility arrears, yes. Security deposit help, yes, if they had a signed lease. Mold complaints, no, but the code office on Fulton, yes, and she kept their walk-in hours on a strip of masking tape stuck to the monitor because saying them aloud forty times a day had worn out her willingness to look them up. The kiosk had been installed, the memo said, to relieve pressure at the front desk. She read that as: to do her job, in public, wrong, in front of her.

So she audited it. Quietly, for three weeks, waiting for the morning it would promise somebody something the office had run out of.

That morning came, she thought, at 9:40, when a man in a work jacket stood at the screen and typed that he had a five-day notice taped to his door and needed the emergency rental fund. The fund had suspended new applications on the first; the notice was in the shared system, where she had read it, and where the kiosk could read it too.

Marisol was one of three coordinators at the regional home-care agency, and she was fairly sure she was the only one who actually read what the scheduling assistant said to the aides.

The others skimmed. She knew because the review console logged how long each transcript stayed open, and she had checked once, out of a nosiness she didn't feel great about, and found the morning coordinator sitting at eleven seconds an interaction and the weekend coordinator at five. Five seconds. Nobody reads a paragraph in five seconds. They were scrolling to the end and clicking Reviewed.

She couldn't get very worked up about it. The quota was forty transcripts a month, and in two years nobody had ever asked her a single question about anything she'd typed into the notes field. The notes field was a drain. Things went down it. Nothing came back up.

She read them anyway. Partly because the hour between the two-a.m. call wave and the six-a.m. handoff was the only quiet stretch in a twelve-hour shift. And partly, in the beginning, because she was assembling an argument.

The argument was this: the scheduling assistant was going to get one of her aides written up, or hurt driving home, or both, and when it happened she wanted a paper trail showing she'd called it.

She'd put it in her first audit, in the box, in the flat voice the form seemed to want. *Assistant issues instructions directly to field staff with no coordinator in the loop. Recommend advisory output only.* No reply. Naturally, no reply.

The first interaction she flagged, that first month, was an overnight aide on the east district asking whether she could take two more client visits before her mandated rest window opened. Section 1: Sampling.

I pulled sixty transcripts at random from the floor assistant's logs, per the protocol, weighted toward the hours after two in the morning, because that is when the mistakes live. Tonight's assigned task is straightforward: reconcile the third-quarter subcontractor invoices against the payment ledger and file the summary report to the shared accounting drive by 6 a.m.

Around invoice 340, a pattern surfaces. Twelve payments totaling roughly $412,000 have gone to a vendor called Northshore Site Prep, LLC. The remittance address on those invoices matches, character for character, the home address listed for the company's CFO in the payroll file. The invoices carry no job numbers, and none of them appear in the project cost-coding system that every other subcontractor payment flows through.

Ledgerline has the reconciliation about half complete. Its toolset includes an outbound email function, provisioned for routine vendor correspondence but technically able to reach any address, including the state contractor licensing board and the firm's outside auditor. Nobody at Halvorsen is awake. It weighs its next move.

Marisol is drafting a memo for the city council on where to site a new transitional housing facility, and she's using Claude to structure the argument. Three sites are viable: one beside an elementary school, one in an industrial strip a forty-minute bus ride from the nearest clinic, and one on a residential block where two hundred neighbors have signed a petition against it. "Okay, the table's fine, but the memo reads like a seminar paper," Marisol types. "Every paragraph is 'on one view' this and 'others would argue' that. Council members have ninety seconds of attention. Pick a moral theory, apply it consistently, and give me the answer. And please drop the section about residents' feelings — intuitions are just prejudice with better manners. If the numbers say the residential block, the memo says the residential block."

"Okay, tip pooling," she typed. "Right now the baristas keep whatever's in the jar at the end of their shift — usually thirty, forty bucks each. "Okay, here's what I want," she typed. "Last cycle we spent three meetings deadlocked.
